text.p: Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said on Sunday stopping work on a Jewish settlement in East Jerusalem would not be on his agenda for a summit in Egypt on the crisis in Middle East peacemaking.
"It is not on the agenda -- not on mine," Netanyahu told Israel Army Radio, two days before he was due to meet Egyptian President Hosni Mubarak at Egypt's Red Sea resort of Sharm el-Sheikh.

Israel's Yedioth Ahronoth daily said the summit was in danger of being cancelled because of Israel's refusal to agree ahead of time to stop building the Har Homa settlement on an East Jerusalem hilltop called Jabal Abu Ghneim by Palestinians.
But in Cairo, Egyptian Foreign Minister Amr Moussa said his country was not considering scrapping the meeting for now and was waiting for the outcome of envoy Osama el-Baza's visit to Israel.
Mubarak sent Baz to Jerusalem to meet Netanyahu's advisers and prepare the ground for the summit.

On Saturday, Israel Television reported that Israel would offer to suspend work once basic infrastructure was completed and press ahead with building homes for Arabs in East Jerusalem. Israeli officials said there would be no such proposal.
Netanyahu's green light to bulldozers to break ground at the site on March 18 plunged Israel-PLO relations into deep crisis and led to the suspension of peace talks.

Palestinians fear the project for 6,500 homes for Jews will complete a ring of Israeli settlements around annexed East Jerusalem, cutting it off from the rest of the West Bank and cementing the Jewish state's hold on all of the city.

Netanyahu spokesman David Bar-Illan said the goal of the summit was to revive peacemaking but he emphasised Israel would not stop settlement building and would stick to its demand the Palestinian Authority do more to curb "terrorism".

"The real message is that we want to resume talks with the Palestinians...but it is quite clear that our insistence on action against terrorism and violence must be the first item on the agenda," Bar-Illan said.
In the radio interview, Netanyahu said Arab leaders "know how to appreciate a strong stand, and this appreciation can lead to progress and compromise by both sides".
Palestinian President Yasser Arafat told reporters in Gaza he hoped the summit would succeed, calling the peace process a vital Palestinian interest.
"Despite all the obstacles (the) peace process is our strategic target and we have to do all our best to save it and to protect it," Arafat said.
But other Palestinians were pessimistic that Egypt, which became the first Arab state to make peace with Israel in a 1979 treaty, would succeed in reviving peace negotiations.
"We are not optimistic...because of Israel's refusal to halt settlement activities," Palestinian Information Minister Yasser Abed Rabbo told Reuters.

"Egypt understands our position very well and it will not fall victim to Israel's tricks of promising to slow down settlement activities while on the ground it would continue to build the infrastructure of Jabal Abu Ghneim," Abed Rabbo said.

Netanyahu's office declined to comment on a report by Britain's Sunday Times that Netanyahu sought the summit with Mubarak after Israeli intelligence warned him of a danger of war with Arab states if settlement building continued.
Israel captured East Jerusalem in the 1967 Middle East war and says it will never cede any part of the city.
Palestinians want East Jerusalem as capital of a future state. They view settlement building as pre-empting final peace talks at which the city's fate is to be negotiated.
